content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's ownership-claim definition ('cause, appoint, or acknowledge as holy — removed from common status, placed under an owner's claim for an appointed purpose, and treated or prepared accordingly') is the only supplied definition that carries every printed use without exception. The dominant systematic reading — sanctification as the Spirit's progressive moral transformation of believers — cannot be the word's meaning in the very texts the book prints: God sanctifies the firstborn with the explanation 'it is mine' (Ex 13:2; Num 8:17); the Father sanctifies Christ and Christ sanctifies Himself with nothing sinful to remove (John 10:36; 17:19); believers sanctify the LORD Himself (Isa 8:13) and God sanctifies His own Name (Ezek 36:23); an unbelieving spouse is sanctified without conversion (1 Cor 7:14); and Hebrews 10:29 supplies the antonym — the sanctified blood counted 'an unholy [common] thing' — proving the operative axis is holy-versus-common, not pure-versus-impure or good-versus-evil. The book does not deny the moral dimension; it locates it correctly as the required outworking of the claim (1 Thess 4:3-7; 2 Tim 2:21), which explains why once-for-all sanctification (Heb 10:10) and prayed-for complete sanctification (1 Thess 5:23) coexist without contradiction. The strongest counter — that qadash/hagiazō is polysemous, with a distinct moral-transformative sense in soteriological contexts alongside the cultic consecration sense — agrees with the book on the root referent and explains the same texts only by splitting the word into two senses where the book's single definition suffices; it is the weaker explanation on parsimony and cannot handle the counterfeit uses (sanctifying war, Jer 6:4; a solemn assembly for Baal, 2 Kings 10:20; idolaters sanctifying themselves, Isa 66:17) as cleanly as 'solemn claim and appointment, whose owner the context identifies.'","book_core_identification":"To sanctify is to cause, appoint, or acknowledge someone or something as holy — removing it from common status and placing it under an owner's claim for an appointed purpose, to be treated and prepared accordingly. God sanctifies by claiming for Himself and fitting for His use; people sanctify God and His Name by treating and displaying Him as holy. Moral cleansing and obedient living fit a person to the holy calling but are not the root meaning of the word.","book_secondary_elaborations":["The three-way distinction between sanctification (common→holy), cleansing (unclean→clean), and justification (accused→judged right), grounded in Leviticus 10:10 and Ezekiel 22:26 and demonstrated in 1 Corinthians 6:11.","The reverse direction of the verb: humans sanctify God and God sanctifies His own Name (Isa 8:13; Ezek 36:23; 1 Pet 3:15).","The claim that even 'dedication to God' is too narrow, since the same verb marks counterfeit or hostile appointments (Jer 6:4; 2 Kings 10:20; Isa 66:17).","The reconciliation of once-for-all sanctification (Heb 10:10) with progressive completion (1 Thess 5:23) as claim-established versus claimed-person-conformed.","The identification of 'common/profane' as the antonym of holy via Hebrews 10:29."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"A polysemy reading drawn from the common interpretation: qadash/hagiazō carries an original cultic sense — to consecrate or set apart for sacred use (Gen 2:3; Ex 29; 1 Tim 4:5) — from which a distinct moral-spiritual sense developed, so that in soteriological contexts (Rom 6:19-22; 1 Thess 4:3-7; 2 Thess 2:13) 'sanctification' genuinely means the Spirit's transformative work of making believers morally holy, not merely the outworking of an ownership claim. On this view the book flattens two real senses into one, and Paul's ethical uses show inward moral renewal is part of the word's meaning in those contexts, not just its consequence.","counter_core_identification":"Sanctification is being set apart as holy for God, with the term in New Testament believer-contexts denoting specifically the Holy Spirit's ongoing moral and spiritual transformation of the believer toward Christlikeness — a distinct lexical sense alongside the older cultic consecration sense.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"SAME_CORE_BROADER","material_core_denial":"To materially contradict the book, the counter would have to deny that removal-from-common-status under God's ownership claim is the word's root and unifying meaning, and assert instead that moral transformation is itself constitutive of the word's meaning in believer-contexts rather than the appointed outworking of the claim. Both readings agree on the referent 'set apart as holy to God'; the counter disputes whether the moral-process component is inside or downstream of the definition.","counter_case":["Paul equates 'your sanctification' directly with concrete moral conduct — abstaining from fornication, possessing one's vessel in honor (1 Thess 4:3-7) — suggesting moral content belongs to the word's meaning in such contexts, not merely its consequence.","Romans 6:19-22 presents sanctification as the fruit of yielding members to righteousness, a process vocabulary that fits transformation.","The prayer that God 'sanctify you completely,' spirit, soul, and body (1 Thess 5:23), reads naturally as pervasive inward renewal.","Standard lexicography and nearly all Christian traditions recognize a developed moral-spiritual sense of hagiazō distinct from bare cultic consecration, so a two-sense analysis has broad scholarly precedent.","Ephesians 5:26 pairs sanctifying with cleansing by washing, suggesting purification is bound into the New Testament use."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Explains sanctification of the sinless Christ (John 10:36; 17:19) — appointment to a mission, not removal of impurity — which any purification- or transformation-rooted definition cannot.","Explains the reverse direction: sanctifying the LORD Himself (Isa 8:13; 1 Pet 3:15) and God sanctifying His own Name before the nations (Ezek 36:23) as acknowledgment and display of the holy claim.","Explains sanctified things that cannot repent — the seventh day (Gen 2:3), food (1 Tim 4:5), the temple's gold and the altar's gift (Matt 23:17,19), vessels (2 Tim 2:21).","Explains 1 Cor 7:14 (unbelieving spouse sanctified, children holy) without asserting moral conversion of the unbeliever — the household falls under the covenant claim.","Explains the firstborn texts where God defines His own act: 'it is mine' (Ex 13:2), 'I sanctified them for myself' (Num 8:17) — ownership language, not transformation language.","Explains Hebrews 10:29's antonym: the apostate counts the sanctifying blood 'a common thing,' fixing holy-versus-common as the operative axis.","Explains counterfeit uses — sanctify war (Jer 6:4; Joel 3:9), a solemn assembly for Baal (2 Kings 10:20), self-sanctifying idolaters (Isa 66:17) — which even 'dedication to the true God' cannot carry.","Preserves Paul's three distinct verbs in 1 Cor 6:11 (washed, sanctified, justified) as three operations rather than redundant synonyms, consistent with Lev 10:10's dual axes.","Reconciles definitive (Heb 10:10 'once for all') and progressive (1 Thess 5:23) texts under one definition: claim established, then the claimed person fitted fully to it.","Coheres with the accepted prior findings on works, righteousness, and justification, which likewise distinguish a word's root meaning from its doctrinal deployment."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Matches the majority lexical and theological tradition, which recognizes a developed moral-spiritual sense of hagiazō in believer-contexts.","Reads 1 Thess 4:3-7 most directly: sanctification simply is holy conduct in that sentence, without needing the claim/outworking distinction.","Accommodates Ephesians 5:26's pairing of sanctifying with cleansing as evidence that purification is intertwined with New Testament sanctification.","Requires no single definition to stretch across cultic, christological, doxological, and ethical uses — polysemy absorbs each context locally."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Exodus 13:2 with Numbers 8:17 — God defines His own sanctifying act as ownership: 'it is mine… I sanctified them for myself.'","John 10:36 and 17:19 — the sinless Christ is sanctified and sanctifies Himself, excluding purification or moral improvement as the root meaning.","Isaiah 8:13; Ezekiel 36:23; 1 Peter 3:15 — humans sanctify God and God sanctifies His Name, uses no transformation-based definition can carry.","Hebrews 10:29 — the antonym of sanctified is 'common,' fixing the holy/common axis, corroborated by Leviticus 10:10 and Ezekiel 22:26.","1 Corinthians 7:14 — an unbelieving spouse is sanctified without conversion.","Genesis 2:3; 1 Timothy 4:5; Matthew 23:17,19; 2 Timothy 2:21 — days, food, gold, and vessels are sanctified though incapable of moral change.","Jeremiah 6:4; 2 Kings 10:20; Isaiah 66:17 — the same verb marks counterfeit appointments, showing the word names a solemn claim whose owner context supplies.","Hebrews 10:10 beside 1 Thessalonians 5:23 — once-for-all and completing uses reconciled under one definition."],"unresolved_objections":["Whether in a few Pauline texts (e.g., 1 Thess 4:3-4; Rom 6:19-22) 'sanctification' has genuinely absorbed moral-purity content into its lexical sense, rather than naming the claim whose required outworking is that conduct — a live lexicographic question that the book answers plausibly but not incontestably.","Ephesians 5:26's tight pairing of 'sanctify and cleanse' shows the operations regularly co-occur; the book distinguishes them, but the frequency of overlap gives the transformation reading some residual footing in believer-contexts.","The book's entry does not adjudicate how far the definitive/progressive theological schema should be retained as doctrine once the lexical core is fixed; that systematic question remains open beyond the word study."],"confidence":"high"}
